title: Interpreting fictional counting data
text:
Audience and outcomes
Audience: upper-division undergraduates beginning health physics. Prerequisites: algebra, unit conversion, square roots, and an introductory explanation of variance and independent random variables. Duration: 60 minutes plus 20 minutes for individual completion. Use a calculator or accessible spreadsheet.
Learners will calculate gross, background, and net count rates; propagate independent counting uncertainties; compare precision without claiming accuracy; and explain the limits of a signed net estimate.

title: Interpreting fictional counting data
text:
Student handout

Model
Gross counts include a signal plus background. Each gross/background pair contains separate independent Poisson counts with constant expected rates during the intervals. Assume the background rate represents the background component of its paired gross record. Times are exact in minutes. Use each observed count as the estimate of its Poisson variance. This plug-in uncertainty estimate is not an exact confidence interval.
For gross count \(G\) over \(t_g\) minutes and background count \(B\) over \(t_b\) minutes:
\[R_g=G/t_g,\qquad R_b=B/t_b,\qquad R_n=R_g-R_b.\]
The estimated standard uncertainty from counting statistics alone is:
\[u(R_n)=\sqrt{G/t_g^2+B/t_b^2}.\]
Rates and their standard uncertainties are in counts per minute, or cpm. Subtracting the estimated background does not remove its uncertainty: independent variance contributions add. Background subtraction and propagation are discussed in DOE Module 2.03, sections F–G. The linear uncorrelated-input rule is described in NIST’s uncertainty guidance.

Each row has its own independent background record; do not pool or reuse background records.

Questions

Calculate gross, background, and net rates and the net standard uncertainty for every row. Show one full substitution with units. Retain extra digits during calculation; report final rates and uncertainties to one decimal place.
For A and B, calculate \(100u(R_n)/|R_n|\). Which has lower relative counting uncertainty? Explain the effect of the fourfold times in this constructed example. Does this establish greater accuracy?
Explain the negative net estimate for C, retaining its sign. Do not replace it with zero or call it negative physical emissions.
Write a 60–100-word explanation for a non-specialist that reports A and states at least two interpretation limits, including whether a dose can be calculated.

No response calibration, radiation type or energy, or exposure context is supplied. Instrument effects, geometry, timing uncertainty, and background variability are outside the model. Do not infer dose, declare presence or absence, set a detection limit, assess compliance, or recommend an operational action.

title: Interpreting fictional counting data
text:
Worked answers
For A, \(R_n=900/5-400/10=180-40=140\) cpm.
\[u(R_n)=\sqrt{900/5^2+400/10^2}=\sqrt{36+4}=6.3246\ \mathrm{cpm}.\]
The variance terms are in cpm squared in this counting model. The square root returns cpm. Report 140.0 ± 6.3 cpm, with ± representing one estimated standard uncertainty from counting alone, not a specified confidence interval.

For B, \(u=\sqrt{3600/20^2+1600/40^2}=\sqrt{10}=3.1623\) cpm. Relative uncertainties are 4.52% for A and 2.26% for B. With identical observed rates and fourfold times, this model gives half the counting standard uncertainty. It does not show removal of bias or establish greater accuracy.
For C, \(u=\sqrt{180/5^2+400/10^2}=\sqrt{11.2}=3.3466\) cpm. Report −4.0 ± 3.3 cpm. Independent fluctuations can produce a gross rate below the estimated background. The signed subtraction result is not a negative physical emission rate. No validated presence/absence decision rule is provided.
Example communication note:

Fictional record A gives a background-subtracted rate of 140.0 cpm with an estimated counting standard uncertainty of 6.3 cpm. The model assumes independent Poisson counts, fixed times, and representative background. It includes counting variation but excludes calibration and other instrument effects. Counts per minute describe recorded events per unit time; the information supplied does not establish dose or support a safety or compliance conclusion. Smaller counting uncertainty alone would not establish greater accuracy.

Accessible individual option
All data are selectable text, equations, and a labeled table; no color or equipment manipulation is required. Plain-text formulas are net = G/tg - B/tb and uncertainty = sqrt(G/tg^2 + B/tb^2). Learners may submit a text solution or accessible spreadsheet with formulas and a written interpretation. Individual written work substitutes for pair discussion without changing the outcomes or rubric. Formal accommodations follow the offering institution’s actual process.
The DOE handbook is a historical technical reading, not current legal or site guidance. The fictional data, questions, worked answers, and rubric are newly composed educational examples.

title: Teaching
text:
Proposed teaching approach
I aim to connect technical concepts with the decisions learners encounter in practice. A lesson should make its learning outcomes clear, give students a structured opportunity to apply the material, and use feedback to identify where understanding needs to improve.
In a proposed health physics lesson, I would ask learners to explain their reasoning, identify information that is missing, and distinguish a justified conclusion from an assumption. Assessment would consider both technical accuracy and the clarity of that reasoning.
I would use a short initial response to identify misconceptions, give learners an opportunity to discuss and revise an explanation, and close with an individual assessment tied to the lesson’s objective. A rubric would make the basis for feedback visible. This proposed sequence is illustrated in the fictional samples above.

title: Teaching
text:
Sample case-based lesson
Proposed instructional example. This fictional scenario is not drawn from an employer, student, incident, or facility.
Topic: Evaluating a radiation safety training plan.
Learning outcomes: Identify the information needed to evaluate a training plan; distinguish attendance from evidence of learning; propose a measurable learning assessment.
Scenario: A fictional teaching laboratory records training attendance but has no assessment of whether learners can explain the procedures presented. A supervisor asks whether attendance records establish that the training is effective.
Activity: In small groups, students list what the available evidence supports, identify unanswered questions, and design one short assessment tied to a stated learning outcome. Groups then explain the limits of their proposal.
Assessment: An individual exit response states one conclusion supported by the scenario, one missing piece of evidence, and one measurable assessment item. A proposed rubric considers evidence use, alignment with the learning outcome, and clarity.
The sample materials demonstrate proposed design choices. They do not establish learner outcomes or substitute for course evaluations, peer observations, or other evidence from instruction already delivered.

title: Research
text:
Doctoral scholarly project
Improving Radiation Safety Compliance Through Standardized In-Person Safety Training for University X-ray Operators
EdD, Public Health Policy, Nebraska Methodist College, July 2026.
Baynum, Christina Hewett. (2026). Improving Radiation Safety Compliance Through Standardized In-Person Safety Training for University X-ray Operators. Doctoral scholarly project, Nebraska Methodist College.
Read the full doctoral project on the college’s website
The project evaluated a one-hour standardized in-person X-ray safety training session using pre- and post-training knowledge assessments and confidence surveys. Eight participants completed paired knowledge assessments. The report describes mean scores increasing from 52.5% before training to 100% shortly afterward, with a paired-samples result of t(7) = 6.16, p < .001.
These are short-term assessment findings from a small group without a comparison group. Confidence outcomes could not be adequately evaluated because only one post-training confidence survey was returned. The design did not establish long-term retention, changes in workplace performance, improved regulatory compliance, or superiority to online training. The report is a publicly available doctoral scholarly project; it is not presented here as a peer-reviewed journal article.
This work provides a starting point for questions about how educational measures should match the conclusions a study can support. The proposed directions below build on that focus; they do not imply that the doctoral project validated a radiation protection program or established the superiority of one teaching format.

title: Research
text:
Proposed research agenda
The following directions describe future research interests. They are not completed studies, funded projects, or established partnerships.

A proposed first study
Proposed research concept.
Question: How can an assessment distinguish recall of radiation safety information from reasoning about a fictional scenario?
Approach: An initial phase would review educational evidence, define a narrow learning objective, and draft aligned knowledge and scenario questions. A proposed rubric would distinguish a correct answer from an explanation supported by the information available. Expert review and a limited pilot, if approved and feasible, would examine whether the questions and scoring criteria are understandable and useful.
Feasibility: The design would begin with original fictional materials. Participant recruitment, any data collection, and use of responses would depend on institutional review, permission, and appropriate arrangements for voluntary participation. No student group, employer data, or research partner is committed.
Possible outputs: An assessment blueprint, draft question set, scoring rubric, and a report of feasibility findings and limitations. Those findings would determine whether a larger study or manuscript was justified. This concept does not promise validation, demonstrated learning gains, or improved workplace safety.


Radiation protection program evaluation
How can radiation protection programs define and evaluate useful indicators of performance? Proposed work would examine candidate measures and the limits of available evidence before testing associations with program outcomes.


Radiation safety education
How should training connect technical understanding with decisions in practice? Proposed studies would evaluate learning and application using defined outcomes and appropriate research approvals.


Implementation and policy
How do organizations translate radiation protection requirements into routine practice? This direction would connect health physics with public health policy and program evaluation.

title: Applied radiation protection
text:
Audience and format
Upper-division undergraduates beginning health physics or a related technical subject. Prerequisites are introductory physics, algebra, unit conversion, and descriptive statistics. A short review introduces independent random variables and variance before the quantitative exercise.
The proposed format is six weeks, with one two-hour class meeting and approximately two hours of independent work per week. No credit value is assigned. Students need a calculator or accessible spreadsheet and a way to submit text-based work. No radiation source handling, instrument operation, or employer data collection is involved.

title: Applied radiation protection
text:
Course purpose
Connect introductory radiation protection concepts with careful interpretation of measurement information. Students practice calculations, identify assumptions, distinguish counting precision from accuracy, and communicate what the evidence supports. Conceptual discussions do not prescribe real-world controls or operational decisions.

title: Applied radiation protection
text:
Measurable learning outcomes
By the end of the proposed course, learners should be able to:

Distinguish recorded count rate, activity, and dose concepts, explaining why they are not interchangeable.
Calculate gross, background, and net rates and estimated counting standard uncertainty under stated assumptions.
Identify limitations and unsupported conclusions in a fictional measurement summary.
Design an assessment item aligned with a measurable safety-education learning outcome.
Write a concise explanation for a non-specialist with explicit evidence limits.

These freely accessible primary sources were checked on 9 November 2026. No textbook purchase is required in this proposed design.

R3: DOE, DOE-HDBK-1122-2009 Part 5, Module 2.03 sections F–G, printed pages 2.03-21–26, on background and uncertainty propagation. This historical technical reference does not set current course, legal, or site procedures.
R4: NIST, Combining uncertainty components, uncorrelated linear-input example and standard uncertainty meaning.
R5: Proposed fictional case lesson, original teaching example used to discuss assessment design.
